_readme: Set 114 Session 3 — the cross-language parity corpus for the step
checklist's row builder.
Session 3 renders an in-flight session's steps in the Work Explorer.
The Explorer is TypeScript, the checklist is Python, and Set 114 S2's
routed ai-assignment.md is explicit about the one acceptable way to
bridge them: 'port the rule with a shared fixture that proves the two
agree row-for-row'. This is that fixture.
TWO suites assert against it, and neither one owns it:
ai_router/tests/test_step_row_parity.py
writes each case to a tmpdir and drives the real
session_checklist.build_rows / read_spec_steps.
tools/dabbler-ai-orchestration/src/test/suite/sessionStepModel.test.ts
drives providers/sessionStepModel.ts's buildStepRows /
parseSpecSteps over the same inputs.
So: change Python alone and the Python test fails. Change TypeScript
alone and the TypeScript test fails. Change this file alone and BOTH
fail. There is no edit that silently diverges the two.
expectedRows is the RENDERED row list in order. expectedSpecSteps is
what spec.md declares for that session, which decides only whether
ordinal reconciliation is trustworthy — it never contributes a row.
NO '<- here' MARKER, in either language (operator ruling 2026-08-11).
Set 120 Session 3 removed it from Python — session_checklist.
HERE_MARKER, its two rendering sites, _mark_here and
ChecklistRow.is_here — because the in-progress status token carries
that fact directly and the marker's single-valued design is what made
it point confidently at the wrong row when the data was bad. That set
could not touch the extension (its standing decision 3), so the
corpus carried an 'isHere' field for the TypeScript half alone and
this _readme declared the divergence.
Set 115 Session 4 finished the removal: markHere, the isHere field
and the tree's HERE_MARKER are gone too, so the field is gone from
these cases and BOTH suites compare the same five fields again. What
an operator reads instead of the marker is the in-progress GLYPH on
the step whose recorded status is in-progress — which is why the
'logged-step-in-flight' case matters: it is the one that pins a real
in-progress row for the icon to come from.
Set 127 Session 2 closed the one-session field-set split S1 opened.
The row model now carries two DERIVED fields — isActive (the step an
in-flight session is currently on) and startedAt (when that step
started) — and both are compared here, in both languages, like every
other field. Neither is read from disk in either language: they are
computed from rows both surfaces already read.
That needed two new inputs, so a case may now declare:
sessionState
the session-state.json content. Python writes it to the case's
tmpdir and session_checklist.build_rows reads it; TypeScript
passes it to sessionStepModel.sessionFlightFacts, which is the
same function minus the file read. ABSENT means no state file,
which is a real and tested case (no derivation at all).
dateTime, on an entry
log_step writes AFTER a step finishes, so an entry's timestamp
is that step's COMPLETION and the next row's derived start.
The rule that must not regress, and that the negative cases here
pin in both languages: EXACTLY ONE row per session may be derived in
flight, and only while that session genuinely is. A derivation that
marks a step in a closed session, or marks several at once, replaces
'no signal' with 'a wrong signal' — strictly worse, because the
operator would then have a reason to believe it.

cases.name: plan-moved-under-the-session
cases.why: THE PLANTED DEFECT (L-112-1). The spec gained a step after registration, so the seeded plan no longer matches spec.md and the ordinal pass is switched OFF. cases.name: bookkeeping-is-not-a-step-and-does-not-render
cases.why: An entry carrying a `kind` is machinery's record ABOUT the session - several are written at registration, before any work exists. It may not mark a planned step done, and since Set 128 S1 it is not a row at all: a step list renders steps. Rendering it put a `complete` glyph on the path-aware critique - a stage that runs once at the END of a set - minutes after registration, and the operator read it exactly that way. Without this rule a set with pathAwareCritique configured shows a finished stage that has not run.

cases.why: Zero rows in flight is a real answer, and the removed marker could not give it: it fell to the last row and read as a claim that the session was working on it. With the marker gone the operator sees two complete glyphs and no in-progress one, which is the truth.

cases.name: in-flight-is-the-logged-step-not-an-earlier-pending-plan-row
cases.why: The case the removed marker used to get wrong, and the one the in-progress GLYPH now gets right for free. An unstarted planned step 2 sits above a logged step in flight; the old rule had to be TOLD to prefer the logged row, while reading the recorded in-progress status cannot point anywhere else. This is also the corpus's proof that a real in-progress row survives reconciliation, which is what the tree's icon is drawn from. Set 127 S2 adds the state file that makes this the DERIVATION's falsifier too: the session is genuinely in flight, so the active-step rule is armed, and it must still stand down because a row already says in-progress. Two rows claiming to be current is the exact defect the removed `<- here` marker produced; `isActive` is false on every row here, including the pending planned one above the logged step.

cases.name: a-falsy-non-string-kind-is-no-kind-at-all
cases.why: THE PATH-AWARE CRITIQUE'S CATCH (gpt-5.5, Set 114 S3). `kind` is untrusted on-disk data, and Python reads it with `str(x or "")` -- so `0` and `false` are 'no kind', i.e. an ORDINARY LOGGED STEP that may claim a planned row. The TypeScript mirror originally used `String(x ?? "")`, which falls back only on null/undefined and turned those into the literal strings "0" and "false" -- bookkeeping, forbidden from claiming. The two surfaces then disagreed about which row was current and whether a planned step had been executed. No shipping writer emits this, which is exactly why only a second reading lens found it and why it belongs here now: the corpus is what stops it reopening.

cases.name: falsy-non-string-fields-read-as-empty
cases.why: The same coercion class as the case above, on the other string-ish fields. Python's `str(x or "")` turns a falsy non-string `stepKey` / `description` / `status` into the empty string, so such a step is ANONYMOUS (uncollapsible -- two of them are two rows) and its status is unknown rather than the literal text "0". A mirror using `??` would render "0" as a label and as a status token, and would collapse the two rows into one.

cases.name: the-active-step-is-derived-where-the-record-is-silent
cases.why: The whole point of Set 127, in both languages. Step 1 is logged complete and nothing has been logged since, so the record says nothing about where the session is — and the session IS in flight. The lowest-numbered seeded plan row with nothing logged against it (step 2) is derived active, and it is the ONLY one: step 3 is equally unlogged and must not also claim to be current. The start times come off the same pass — step 1 started when the session did, step 2 started when step 1 finished, and step 3, which has not started, carries no time at all rather than its seeded registration stamp (operator ruling 3).

cases.name: a-blocked-row-is-not-overwritten-by-the-derivation
cases.why: The record answering with a STOP, rather than with progress. Step 2 is logged `blocked` in a session that is genuinely in flight. The ledger has already said where this session is, so the derivation stands down entirely — step 1's pending planned row above it does NOT become active, and the blocked row keeps its own token rather than being relabelled in-progress. Both languages box this `[!]` / paint it with the one did-not-go-well glyph. The blocked row also carries NO start: step 1 above it is a planned row nobody ever logged, so it is a step that never finished and it breaks the start-time chain rather than handing the row below it the session's own start.

cases.name: a-prose-status-is-evidence-of-nothing
cases.why: The five legacy prose-in-`status` rows pre-date Set 120 S1's strict writer, and the obligation they create is that the derivation must not TRUST the status field blindly. A planned row carrying prose is not a token either language recognises, so it is not eligible to be the active step — and it does not stop the rule, because `[?]` is a question rather than an answer. The next genuinely-pending planned row is the active one. This is also the falsifier for the mirror's one real trap: TypeScript's `glyphStatusOf` FALLS BACK to `not-started` for an unknown token, so an eligibility test written through it would pick the prose row here and disagree with Python by one row.

cases.name: a-bookkeeping-record-is-transparent-to-the-start-time-chain
cases.why: A `path_aware_critique` / `contract_gate` / `dual_surface_mode` / `suggestion_disposition` entry carries a dateTime, but it is a record ABOUT the session written by machinery - which is why it may not claim a planned row and, since Set 128 S1, is not rendered as a step at all. It must also not act as the previous STEP's completion for the row below it: the second step here starts when the first step finished (09:12), not when the policy record was written (10:00). Driven through the plan-less path with the bookkeeping entry BETWEEN two steps, which is the only place the transparency is observable - if it were merely dropped from the list without being excluded from the chain, step 2 would start at 10:00.

cases.name: a-plan-less-state-file-still-dates-the-first-row
cases.why: A set whose plan is not yet committed writes a v4 file with NO sessions[] ledger and a top-level status / startedAt instead (docs/session-state-schema.md, 'Plan-less carve-out'). Read strictly per-session it would answer 'no start time' for every row and the first row would lose a start the file records explicitly. It contributes its startedAt and NEVER an in-flight claim: the file names no session number to attach a current step to. Nothing is lost by that refusal, because a plan-less set has no `### Session N` headings and therefore no seeded plan rows to derive onto — which is exactly the shape of this case.

cases.name: the-start-time-chain-does-not-read-the-status-vocabulary
cases.why: Set 127 S1 round 2 left one adjudicated-minor residual for this session: an entry's dateTime is read as its step's completion whatever its status says. Settled as BY DESIGN, in both languages at once, and pinned here. `completed` is one of the 15 non-canonical tokens Set 120 S2 deliberately preserved; the renderer boxes it `[?]` because it is not in the table. A chain that only advanced on a RECOGNISED terminal token would silently strip the start times off every legacy set that spells it that way -- and the derivation's own rule is that an unrecognised token is evidence of nothing, which has to cut both ways: it may not be read as evidence of completion, and it may not be read as evidence of non-completion either. What advances the chain is the ENTRY EXISTING: log_step writes when the orchestrator records the step, so its stamp is the last known moment of that step's activity and the best available lower bound for the row below it. The case the residual worried about -- a step still in flight dating the row under it -- cannot mislead in the shape that actually occurs: a row saying in-progress makes the record the answer, so no planned row below it is ever derived active, and a planned row that is not active carries no time at all.
